newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt frees group accused of pushing Shi'ite ideas.
newsitem.headline: Egypt frees group accused of pushing Shi'ite ideas.

text.p: Egypt has set free 56 people accused of promoting ideas of Shi'ism, a branch of Egypt's official religion Islam and the dominant sect in Iran, an Islamist lawyer said on Monday.

The detention of the group late last year and others last month highlights the often tense ties between Sunni Egypt and Shi'ite Iran, which Cairo often accuses of supporting militant groups trying to impose a strict Islamic state in Egypt.

Egyptian newspapers said on Monday one of them, preacher Sheikh Hassan Shehata, was freed after his detention since September for propagating Shi'ite ideas, including the notion of temporary marriage.
"He obtained release yesterday. He had some independent ideas about Islamic law," Shehata's Islamist lawyer Mukhtar Nuah told Reuters. "All (56) of them went."

Neighbours sipping tea outside Shehata's apartment block in a Cairo suburb on Monday said the preacher had not returned. Witnesses had told Reuters after his detention that police took Shehata away at dawn and seized books from his flat.

Shehata is one of at least 65 people Egypt has rounded up since September and accused of promoting Shi'ite ideas. Shi'ism is not illegal in Egypt but the government is wary of any Iranian religious influence.

In the same language it uses for Moslem militants, the interior ministry said it wanted to question the detainees, the most recent taken in January, on suspicion of "subverting the constitution, preventing authorities from enforcing it, harming national unity and social order, and exploiting religion."
Interior Minister Hassan al-Alfi said in Tunis in January that Egyptian "authorities cut communication between them and their counterparts in Iran, which was supporting them in their wicked plans.
Alfi said a number of their organisational papers which were seized contained instructions "to spread sedition, confusion and implement hostile plots."
A security source said the accusations against Shehata were dropped after he "repented". There was no immediate information available from public prosecutor officials about the others.
But diplomats and lawyers had told Reuters their detention reflected Egypt's sometimes strained ties with Shi'ite Iran.
Iran denies the accusations. It says Egypt tries to cover up internal problems rooted in Cairo's pro-Western policies.
"The problem perhaps has no legal basis but expresses the nature of Egyptian-Iranian relations," said Mohamed Andeel, an Egyptian Organisation for Human Rights field work lawyer.
A diplomat, asked about any connection between the detainees and Iran, said that Egypt has accused Iran of being behind an assassination attempt against President Hosni Mubarak in 1995.
He said he saw Egypt's allegation of Iranian influence as made "for political reasons, not real ones".
This month Alfi accused Iran of continuing to support the militant Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group), the largest organisation fighting to overthrow the Egyptian government.
On Monday, President Hosni Mubarak and the head of the Shi'ite Council in Lebanon, Mohammad Mehdi Shamsuddin, held talks on Islamic affairs and the situation in southern Lebanon.

Shehata's followers had said his sermons were moderate and some said he was not a Shi'ite. Shi'ites are a tiny minority believed to be a few hundred in Sunni Egypt. "He was the one who influenced me to wear the head scarf," said one woman.
Shi'ites and Sunnis differ originally over who should have led the Moslem community on Prophet Mohammad's death. Differences in doctrine, law and politics developed.
Nouh's defence included a fatwa from al-Azhar, Egypt's highest religious institution, on the legitimacy of Shi'ism.

"When the air is tense between Egypt and Iran, Egypt goes and arrests Shi'ites. It puts pressure, saying Iran is financing this and that," said Hisham Mubarak, Centre for Human Rights Legal Aid director. "The atmosphere is the same as in 1988."
Egypt that year rounded up at least 23 men for propagating Shi'ite ideas, including temporary marriage, said Nouh.
